sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Inari** ​(*inari*) — ‌Rice, Fertility, ‌Foxes ​· Deity ​of ​rice, sake, ​and fox ​messengers ‌— belongs ​to the ​Japanese ‌tradition, where ​it ‌is catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Rice, Fertility, ​Foxes". The ​name ​means "Rice ​load"[^1].

‌**Inari** is ​one of ‌the ​most widely ‌worshipped kami ​in ‌Japan: a ​deity ‌of rice ​who became, ​over ‌a thousand ‌years, the ‌patron ​of fertility, ​sake, ‌smiths, merchants, ​and worldly ​success. ‌The vermillion ​torii gates ​and ‌fox statues ​of ‌Fushimi Inari ​Taisha in ​Kyōto ​are among ​the most ‌iconic ‌images of ​Japanese ‌religion.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ​name ‌as **Inari** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ​[its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/inari/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ​*inari* survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by ‌the early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in ​Japanese characters ​as ​**稲荷**. ​Etymologically ‌it ​means ​"Rice ‌load"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form *inari* ‌survives ​only ​because ​the ​early ​domain-name ‌system ​could ‌not carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not ​an ‌ancient ‌spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration ​**Inari** ‌recovers ​the ​full ‌diacritic ​detail ​of ‌the scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ​in ​the ​address ​bar. ‌The ‌restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ‌form — ​a ​description ‌computed ‌from ‌the ‌displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**i** ​→ ​**I** ​— ‌Same
- ​**n** ​→ ​**n** — ‌Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ​**a** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**r** ‌→ ​**r** ​— Same
- ​**i** ​→ ‌**i** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is ​**/i.na.ɾi/** ​— Modern ​Standard ​Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**I-** ‌— ​Close front ‌[i]
- ​**-na-** — ‌Alveolar ​nasal [n] ​plus ​open ​central [a]
- ​**-ri** ‌— Alveolar ​tap ‌[ɾ] plus ​close ‌front ​[i]; the ‌name ​is often ‌derived ​from 稲荷 ​'rice ‌load'

‌For the ‌modern ​speaker, the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​'EE-nah-ree' ​— ‌the 'r' ​is ​a light ‌tap, ​and all ‌vowels ​are short.

​Kindred ​and ​historical forms ‌of ‌the name:

- ​**Japanese** ‌— 稲荷 ​(Inari), ​'rice ‌load,' kami ‌of ‌rice, fertility, ‌and ​foxes
- **Alternative ‌etymology** ​— ​From ine-nari, ​'rice-growing' ‌— both ​derivations ​are guesses ​by ‌later ​commentators
- **Messengers** ​— ​Kitsune, the ‌fox ​spirits who ‌serve ​Inari

‌Inari keeps ​its ‌restoration plain: ‌plain ​Hepburn. The ​name's ​significance ​is cultic ‌and ‌agricultural, not ​orthographic.

sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Inari** ​is one ‌of ‌the ​most widely ​worshipped ​kami ​in Japan: ​a ‌deity ​of rice ​who ‌became, ​over a ‌thousand ​years, ‌the patron ​of ​fertility, sake, ​smiths, ​merchants, ​and worldly ‌success. ​The ‌vermillion torii ​gates ‌and ​fox statues ‌of ​Fushimi ‌Inari Taisha ​in ​Kyōto ‌are among ‌the ‌most iconic ​images ​of ‌Japanese religion.[^1]

### ​Rice ​and ‌Harvest

Inari ​governs ​the ‌rice plant ​— ‌enshrined ​as Uka-no-mitama, ​the ​spirit ​of the ‌grain ‌itself.

### ​Fox Messengers

‌Kitsune ​carry the ​kami's ‌messages ‌and hold ‌the ‌granary ​key in ‌their ​statues' ​mouths.

### Merchant ​Success

‌From ​the medieval ​period, ​traders, ‌brewers, and ​smiths ​prayed to ​Inari ‌for ​prosperity.

### Fushimi ‌Inari

​The ‌head shrine ​in ‌Kyōto, ‌founded in ​711 ​CE, ​is ringed ​by ‌mountains ‌of donated ​torii.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Inari ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ​of recurring ‌attributes, ​each ​a compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the name:[^1]

- ​**Vermillion ‌torii ​gates** — ​The ​donated ​gates climbing ​Mount ‌Inari ​— ‌more than ​ten ‌thousand ​— each ‌one ​an ‌invoice of ​a ​fulfilled ‌prayer
- **Fox ‌(kitsune)** ‌— ​The paired ​foxes ‌flanking ​the shrine: ​one ‌bears ​the granary ​key, ‌one ​the ‌jewel; red ​bibs ​mark ​their veneration
- ​**Rice ‌sheaf** ‌— Inari's ​first ‌body ​— the ​plant ‌itself, ‌worshipped as ‌Uka-no-mitama ‌before ​any temple ‌existed
- ​**Jewel** ​— The ​wish-granting ‌gem ​in ​the fox's ​mouth; ‌prosperity ​compressed to ​a ​single ‌stone
- **Fried ​tofu ‌(abura-age)** ​— The ‌offering ​said ‌to please ‌the ​fox ​— hence ​the ​sushi ‌that bears ‌Inari's ​name

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Inari has no single ​canonical myth cycle in the Kojiki manner. The ‌kami's identity is distributed across **a charter ‌legend, a shifting triad of enshrined gods, the ​fox lore of the medieval period, and ​the craft legends of the cities** — ​a biography written by worshippers rather than scribes.[^1]

### ​The Rice-Cake That Flew (The Foundation)

The ​Nihon Shoki (Wadō 4, 711 CE) tells how ‌**Hata no Irogu**, a leader of the ​immigrant Hata clan, practiced archery on a mountain ​by setting up a rice-cake as a ‌target. When his arrow struck it, the cake ​rose into the air as a white ‌bird and flew to the summit, where ​a radiance appeared. Taking this as a divine ‌sign, Irogu founded a shrine on the ​spot. Rice-cake, white bird, mountain light: the kami ​announced itself through its own substance. The ​Hata were continental immigrants — weavers, engineers, and ​shrine-builders — and their mountain cult folded ​the new rice technology into the older kami ‌world. The date makes Inari's shrine among ​the oldest documented in Japan, and the ‌legend is the charter of what became Fushimi ​Inari Taisha. It is already the whole ‌theology of Inari — a deity who arrives ​riding the rice itself.[^2]

### Three Gods, One ‌Kami (The Triad)

At its head shrine, Inari ​is not one deity but three: **Uka-no-mitama**, ‌the spirit of the rice plant; **Satahiko**; and ​**Ōmiyanome**, the ancestral weaver and food-goddess. Other ​Inari shrines substitute **Toyouke**, the goddess of ‌the Ise Grand Shrine's outer precinct, who prepares ‌the food of the gods. Medieval oracles ‌ratified the triad, and the three remain enshrined ​today. Even the kami's gender never settled: ​Inari appears as an aged man, a radiant ‌woman, or a fox-mounted deva, depending on ​the shrine and the century. Scholars read the ​fluidity as the mark of a genuinely ‌popular cult, indifferent to the tidy genealogies ​of the court chronicles: Inari names less a ​person than an office, the power that ‌fills the granary. The many-faced kami mirrors the ​many fates of rice — seedling, grain, ‌sake, wealth — each a different disguise of ​one sustenance.

### The Messengers of the Granary ​(The Fox)

By the medieval period the ​**kitsune** — the fox — had become Inari's ​recognized messenger, and by the Edo period ‌Inari cult and fox cult were so entangled ‌that temple regulations had to forbid offerings ​of fried tofu at certain times. Foxes carried ‌the kami's messages, guarded the granary keys ​held in their statues' mouths, and appeared in ​dreams and possession cults. The thousands of ‌vermillion torii at Fushimi Inari, each donated ‌by a shop or a family, map the ‌commercial empire of a deity whose messenger ‌moves, like trade itself, silently at the margins ​of the night. In the fox, Inari ‌acquired what few agricultural gods possess: a double, ​clever and dangerous, who could walk into ​the human world and speak with a human ​voice. Tales multiplied of fox-weddings glimpsed in ‌the rain, of possessed mediums channeling the ​kami, and of the nine-tailed fox whose tails ​count its centuries.

### The Smith's Dream (The ​Forge)

A tenth-century legend tells of **Munechika**, the ‌Kyōto swordsmith ordered to forge a blade ​for the emperor with no partner to work ​the bellows. In a dream Inari promised ​help; a mysterious youth appeared, and before dawn ‌two swords stood completed — one for ​the court, one kept by the smith. ‌The tale, dramatized in the Nō play *Kokaji*, ​rests on the smith's dedication of his ‌forge to Inari. The kami of the grain ​was equally the kami of the craft: ‌rice becomes sake, and iron becomes a sword, ‌by the same alchemy of transformation. The ​blades of the legend remain treasured names, and ​Munechika's Sanjō school of smiths flourished for ​generations at the capital. Inari's patronage of ​smiths, brewers, and merchants is the medieval extension ‌of the oldest fact about the deity ‌— that the stored harvest is capital, and ​capital wants a god.

sources.citation: Kojiki (rice-kami genealogies).
Smyers, The Fox and the Jewel: Shared and Private Meanings in Contemporary Japanese Inari Worship.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Inari ​is the ‌great syncret ‌of ​Japanese religion. ​Medieval Tendai ​identified ​the kami ​with **Dakiniten**, ‌the ​fox-riding deva ​absorbed from ‌Indian tantra, ​and ‌esoteric lineages ​placed Inari ‌within ​mandala systems ​of the ​five ​grains. The ​Muromachi and ‌Edo ​periods saw ‌Inari conflated ​with ‌Benzaiten and ​with Uka-no-mitama's ‌Buddhist ​guises; fox-possession ‌cults and ​Inari ​mediums blurred ‌the shrine ‌and the ‌street. ​No figure ​in Japan ‌tolerated ​layered identity ​more gracefully ‌— ​male or ​female, one ‌or ​three, kami ‌or buddha. ​When ​the Meiji ​state ordered ​the ‌separation of ‌Shinto and ​Buddhism, ‌Inari shrines ​quietly stored ​their Buddhist ‌statuary ‌away; most ‌of it ‌returned ​within a ‌generation.[^1]

Kindred ​figures ​in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index ​include [[benzaiten|Benzaiten]] ​(fortune, harvest, ​and ‌abundance), [[ebisu|Ebisu]] ​(japanese fortune ​and ​harvest deities), ‌[[anahita|Anāhitā]] (earth ​/ ‌mother / ​fertility), [[audhumla|Auðhumla]] ‌(earth / ​mother ‌/ fertility), ‌[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] (earth ​/ ​mother / ​fertility), and ​[[bastet|Bꜣstt]] ‌(earth / ‌mother / ​fertility).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Fushimi ​Inari ‌Taisha, ‌rebuilt ​after the ​Ōnin ​War ​and ​crowned ‌with ​its ​endless ‌gates, is ​among ‌the ​most ‌visited ​religious ​sites ​on ​earth, and ​the ‌estimates ​of ‌thirty ​thousand ‌Inari ​shrines ‌across Japan ​exceed ‌any ​other ​deity's. ‌The ‌kami ‌guards ​restaurants, rice ​merchants, ‌and ​corporate ​headquarters; ‌the ​sushi ​named ‌for the ​fox, ‌inari-zushi, ​is ​sold ​in ​every ‌convenience ‌store; and ​the ‌fox-mask ​of ​festival ‌stalls ‌is ‌recognizably ‌Inari's. In ​a ‌secular ​age, ​Inari ​prospers ‌as ​the ​most pragmatic ​divinity ‌in ​the ​pantheon: ​pray, ‌work, ​and ‌share the ​result ‌— ​the ‌god ‌of ​the ​harvest ​became the ​god ‌of ‌the ​hustle.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Fushimi ​Inari ‌Taisha ‌in ​southern Kyōto ​has ​been ​Inari's ​head ‌shrine ​since ​711 ‌CE. ​Burned in ‌the ​Ōnin ‌War ​(1468) ​and ​rebuilt ​by ​the ‌late fifteenth ​century, ‌its ​main ‌halls, ​its ‌tunnel-paths ​of ‌donated ​torii — ​over ‌ten ‌thousand ‌strong, ​dating ​chiefly ‌from ​the ​Edo period ‌onward ​— ​and ‌the ​mountain-top ‌okusha ​shrines ​form one ​of ​Japan's ‌best-documented ‌cult ​landscapes. ‌Excavations ​and ​shrine ‌records trace ‌the ‌cult's ‌growth ​from ‌a ​Hata-clan ​agricultural ​shrine ‌to the ​devotional ​center ​of ‌a ​national ​commercial ​network, ‌and ​the thousands ‌of ​subsidiary ‌Inari ​shrines ‌preserve ‌medieval ​siting ​patterns ​at field ​boundaries ‌and ‌village ​entrances.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Inari ​teaches that ‌the ‌sacred is ​not ​separate from ​the ​everyday. The ​rice in ‌the ​bowl, the ​sake ‌in the ​cup, ‌the ledger ​of ‌the shop, ​the ​contract of ​the ​marriage — ​all ‌flow through ​one deity ‌who ​declines to ‌be ​a single ‌person.

​The fox ‌is ​the perfect ​emblem ‌of this ‌theology: ‌it crosses ​the ​boundary between ‌field and ​village, ​animal and ‌ancestor, ​omen and ​blessing, ‌exactly as ​rice ‌crosses from ​seed ​to wealth. ​To ​modern eyes ‌Inari looks ‌like ​a god ‌of ​capitalism, and ​there ‌is truth ‌in ‌it — ‌Inari ​protected merchants ‌when ​merchants were ​new, ​and prosperity ‌cults follow ​prosperity. ​But the ​older ‌lesson stands ​underneath: ​abundance is ​relational. ‌The granary ​key ‌is entrusted ​to ‌a messenger, ​not ‌a master, ‌and the ​ten ​thousand gates ​are ​not a ‌wall ‌but an ​invitation.[^1]
